::: {.callout-note}
**This document is for the facilitator's eyes only.** It is rendered with the site but left out of the navbar, so nothing on the site links to it. It holds the run sheets, the answer keys, the crib facts and the contingency ladders of the three one-day formats of the EU-frames case: open science (`slides/eu-frames-one-day-open-science.qmd`), data tools (`slides/eu-frames-one-day-data-tools.qmd`) and statistical methods (`slides/eu-frames-one-day-methods.qmd`). All three work on aggregate data only and are taught mainly in the browser lab. The three-day course and the other formats are on [Running the tracks](tracks.qmd).
:::

---

## The three formats {#the-three-formats}

| Format | What it keeps | What it leaves out | Deck |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open science | Credibility, the three Rs, SCORE and Multi100, the infrastructures of open research; the paper, the five analysts and the estimand statement; the reproduction of one of three analysts and the slips in their deposits; replication on new data and a preregistration written and not run | The menu, the class chart, every submission | `eu-frames-one-day-open-science` |
| Data tools | A short credibility opening; the toolchain; R and the IDE; data management on the panel and its checks; the reproduction as the target of the R work; the report, version control and archiving; one look at the curve | The menu, the class chart, every submission | `eu-frames-one-day-data-tools` |
| Methods | The estimand and the causal graph; the reproduction; the three reproduced models, few clusters and CR2; the menu and its tutorial; the class chart with both submissions; the curve, its inference and the declared analysis | The infrastructures of open research and the toolchain, beyond a slide | `eu-frames-one-day-methods` |

Every format runs on the same clock: four parts of ninety minutes, from 10:00 to 18:00 GMT, with breaks of thirty, sixty and thirty minutes. The clock times below are drafts; set them for the delivery and paste them into the day plan.

| Segment | Clock (GMT, draft) |
|---|---|
| Part 1 | 10:00–11:30 |
| Break | 11:30–12:00 |
| Part 2 | 12:00–13:30 |
| Lunch | 13:30–14:30 |
| Part 3 | 14:30–16:00 |
| Break | 16:00–16:30 |
| Part 4 | 16:30–18:00 |

---

## The delivery lifecycle {#delivery-lifecycle}

Between deliveries the landing page advertises no upcoming delivery. Scheduling a delivery takes the steps below, and resetting after one takes two.

**Scheduling.**

- [ ] Fill the `delivery:` block in `_variables.yml` (date, venue or platform, event, mode, registration URL), set `track` to `eu-frames-one-day-open-science`, `eu-frames-one-day-data-tools` or `eu-frames-one-day-methods`, and set `active: 'true'`. Re-render and push, and the landing page shows a "Next delivery" callout. Set `active: 'false'` again afterwards.
- [ ] Decide recording. If recording: talk segments only, announced at the start of each recorded stretch, paused for hands-on and chat-heavy segments. Nothing in the day depends on the recording either way.
- [ ] Methods day only: optionally create the preregistration mirror form from `_planning/prereg-form-spec.md` and paste its URL into `_variables.yml`. The preregistration block is the primary record and the form only a backup, so skipping the form loses nothing.

**Resetting, after a methods day.** The other two formats submit nothing.

- [ ] Export the responses Sheet (File → Download → CSV) and commit it as a date-stamped snapshot (for example `cases/eu-frames/data/class_results_2026-11-06.csv`); refresh `cases/eu-frames/data/class_results.csv` as `facilitator/live-results-setup.md` describes if you want the archived class visible on the site.
- [ ] Clear (or archive to a second tab) the old rows in the live Sheet so that the chart opens almost empty for the next class. **Do not touch the Form, the Worker, or the field schema.** The pipeline works, and only the rows change from one class to the next.

---

## The week before

- [ ] Send joining instructions: the before-the-day page of the track, the browser-lab link with the instruction to open it once, the two-window or two-device tip, and the [case study](../cases/eu-frames/index.qmd) as the pre-reading. Installing R and an IDE is optional in all three formats, and recommended for the data-tools day.
- [ ] Confirm that the four Task 2 instructions on the Multi100 slides match your own Task 2 report (copy in `_planning/osf_source/moreh_rep_vAPR2025/`), which is the source that the slides quote.
- [ ] Open-science day: check that the three OSF deposits of Hands-on 3b load logged out (osf.io/vycgd, osf.io/nz7ka, osf.io/6zqct), and that osf.io/h7432 shows the five Multi100 components.
- [ ] Methods day: click once through the tab switching of Parts 3 and 4 (deck, the specification menu, the decision map, the Multiverse page and back), so that the order is familiar on the day.

## The night before

- [ ] Render the site and push; if the site is published, confirm that the Pages build completes on GitHub Actions.
- [ ] **Browser lab cold load**: open the live page of `cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd` in a private window on the connection typical of the venue; time the load of the webR engine; run the cell of Task 1 and all three cells of Task 3. The first run of the cell of 018OL downloads lme4 and lmerTest, about 32 MB, so time that too.
- [ ] Methods day: **live results loop** (full setup and checks in `facilitator/live-results-setup.md`): submit one anonymous test row through the Form in a private window, confirm that it reaches the Sheet and that the Worker returns the sheet as CSV, press *Run Code* on the live [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) page and find the test mark. Then delete the test row.
- [ ] Methods day: **preregistration loop**: complete the preregistration cell of the browser lab with a dummy specification, run `prereg()`, `build_model()` and `run_spec()`, and check the output. If the mirror form exists, submit one dummy row and delete it.
- [ ] Prepare the catch-up card, the help document and the day plan (texts below) as snippets ready to paste.
- [ ] Charge everything; sign a second device in to the meeting as a participant, to check what the class sees.

## Opening the room {#opening-the-virtual-room--30-minutes-before}

- [ ] Open the meeting early; enable chat for everyone; check that breakout rooms are available (they are optional – nothing depends on them).
- [ ] Seed the chat with the site URL, the browser-lab URL, the cheatsheet URL and the day plan with its times (the standing order if the host drops: "follow the day plan; finish the current task or take the break early; I will rejoin").
- [ ] Post the interaction key: "green circle = working; STUCK = I need help; answers to quizzes: type but hold until I say go".
- [ ] Share the deck; keep the browser lab ready in a second tab (methods day: also the specification menu, the decision map and the Multiverse page).
- [ ] If recording: announce it now and state what is and is not recorded.

---

## Driving the decks {#deck-navigation}

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| space, right arrow, clicker | next slide. **Always exactly one slide** – the decks are set to linear mode so that no clicker press can skip a segment |
| **`d`** | switch between the **extended** and the **lean** deck, live. In lean mode the optional slides are taken out of the deck: every key skips them and the count drops |
| **`]`** and **`[`** | jump to the **next or previous part** |
| **`g`** | **jump bar**: type a few letters of any slide title, press Enter |
| **`s`** | speaker view (notes, timer, next slide) |
| **`f`**, **`esc`** | fullscreen, slide overview |

**The readout, top right,** has two lines. The first names the part and gives the position in the part and in the deck (for example `PART 3`, `8/24`, `90/148`). The second is a badge that is always present and shows the state of the deck:

| Badge | Means |
|---|---|
| green **extended** | the full deck, and this slide is part of the main flow |
| burgundy **optional** | the full deck, and this slide belongs to an optional run. The figure beside it is your position inside that run – `3/12` |
| amber **lean** | the optional runs are switched off |
| a burgundy **dot** before the amber badge | lean mode, and an optional run has been lifted out right here – either the slide you are on is the last before it, or the first after it. Press `d` if the class wants it |

Each deck lifts some optional runs into its main flow: the data-tools deck the tools run of Part 1 and the R tutorial of Part 2, the methods deck the methodological tutorial of Part 3 and the multiverse tutorial of Part 4. The open-science deck carries no optional run in its main flow. Add `?depth=0` to the address to open a deck in lean mode. The first slide of each optional run has a small grey link at the top right, which says how many slides the run contains and where the main flow resumes.

Times in the tables are part-relative, 0:00 being the start of the part; the clock times assume the draft day above.

| Rel. | Segment | What I do | What participants do | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Welcome, the plan, the two kinds of aim, what you do not need (6′) | Premise in two sentences ("*Nature* asked three times whether social science holds up – I was inside one of the papers; today you sit where I sat"). "Open the browser lab NOW and leave it to load." | Open the lab tab; type one word in the chat for why they came. | Late joiners: greet in the chat, never restart. |
| 0:06 | Talk: credibility (18′) | What social science is for; false positives and forking paths; the evidence; incentives and questionable research practices; the red-card study and its twenty-nine estimates; 'replication' crises. | Listen. | The two points of the red-card study that must get across are the blind peer review and the grouping by response distribution. |
| 0:24 | Talk: the vocabulary and open research (12′) | The matrix of data and analysis; repeatability and credibility; the quick check in peer review; the practices of open research. | Chat waterfall on the quick check. | The matrix is the one slide to copy down. |
| 0:36 | Talk: SCORE (18′) | The programme; the three studies, each with its results; the three Rs across SCORE. | Listen. | If behind, cut the slide on data availability to one line. |
| 0:54 | Talk: Multi100 from the inside (14′) | What an analyst received; the paper in brief (define OA here); the two tasks; the common scale; the five-analyst forest **one row at a time**; the software slide. | Watch the reveal. | Never rush the forest reveal. |
| 1:08 | Talk and hands-on: open research infrastructures (12′) | Repositories, archives and registries; the data of the case and their terms; three minutes in the SCORE dossier. | Open osf.io/h7432 and find the deposit of an analyst. | If the OSF is slow, show the dossier on my screen. |
| 1:20 | The browser lab, then Task 1 (10′ and the break) | The lab and the workspace in one slide, what the tools cannot do, then the setup task. Stay on the call through the break for STUCKs. | Task 1 and the warm-up; break. | This is the only point of the day at which a broken machine can be fixed without costing anyone content. |

| 1:30 | Lunch | Lunch slide; post the return time; point to section 3 of the case study. | Lunch. | Lunch is a hard stop. |

Trigger 1:12: Task 4 shortens to two `try_spec()` calls and a submission – but everybody still submits.
- **Part 4** – trigger 0:18: skip the multiverse tutorial, keep "what the curve leaves out". Trigger 0:57: shorten the critics to one slide.

**Never cut:** the five-analyst reveal; the estimand waterfall; the half-built graph and its adjustment set; the reproduction waterfall; the table of CR2 tests; the Task 4 submission; the bet before the decomposition; the preregistration moment.

## Online and in-person cue sheet {#online--in-person-cue-sheet}

The materials are identical online and in person. What changes is how people answer, flag trouble and pair up.

| Beat | Online | In person |
|---|---|---|
| Quiz and waterfall answers | type in the chat, hold until "go" | write on paper, hands up on "go" |
| Working or stuck | green circle or "STUCK" in the chat | green or red sticky notes |
| Roll-call | "raise hand" | visual sweep |
| Pair moments | breakout rooms if available; a chat variant otherwise | table pairs |
| Rescues | buddy-chunk on the shared screen | the facilitator circulates |
| The live chart (methods day) | everyone opens the Multiverse page themselves | projector and own laptops |
| Form links (methods day) | pasted in the chat | QR codes on the slides |
| Breaks | countdown slide and "back at :xx" in the chat | countdown slide and spoken |

---

## Chat protocols and ready-to-paste texts {#chat-protocols-and-ready-to-paste-texts}

**Waterfall:** "Type your answer now but DON'T send – hold it. … Go." Holding the answers back keeps each one independent of the others. For Task 3 the answer is the analyst and the value, for example `KQXUE t = -7.169`, so that the wall of identical values appears once for each analyst.

**Help:** a STUCK in the chat is the first flag. The help document, a shared editable document whose link goes into the chat at the start, is the second place to look and the place where errors get pasted. Check it at the minutes that the run sheet names. Rescues run in the main room by buddy-chunk.

**Silent class:** wait 20 seconds, then take reactions as the minimal response, and name one or two people gently. Two substantive answers from twenty participants are enough to proceed.

**Catch-up card (paste at the start of Part 3):**

> Just back? You missed nothing you can't recover: (1) if Task 2 is unfinished, keep your estimand statement and come back to it later; (2) Task 3 is the reproduction – choose C6HJR, KQXUE or 018OL in the browser lab; each has a hint and a full solution, and the values on record are −3.804, −7.169 and −1.206; (3) flag STUCK and I'll come to you.

**Facilitator-drop standing order (seeded in the chat at the start):**

> If I drop off the call: keep going. The day plan (link) has the timings – finish the current task or take the break early. I will rejoin as soon as I can.

## Contingencies {#contingency-table}

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| **A participant's webR fails mid-task** | The cheatsheet ladder: hard reload and rerun the cells above, then a second browser, then buddy-chunk on my screen. Methods day, last rung: the specification is one row of `cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve.csv`, which the download button on the Multiverse page serves; submit it by hand. |
| **The cell of 018OL stalls on its download** | Let it finish on a good connection, or switch the participant to C6HJR or KQXUE, which need nothing beyond the page. |
| **A participant's installation breaks** | Switch them to the browser lab, which holds every task; the workspace survives for later. |
| **The live chart fails (methods day)** | Rung 1: `cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd` falls back to the committed `cases/eu-frames/data/class_results.csv`. Rung 2: pull the Sheet CSV, commit, re-render locally and share my screen. Rung 3: the static curve of 864 and the reference results are enough for the debrief. |
| **The OSF is slow or unreachable** | Show the dossier and the deposits on my screen. The data never depend on the OSF, because they ship with the browser lab and the workspace. |
| **My connection drops** | The standing order in the chat. |
| **Recording objections** | Recording is optional, so stop it. |

## Expected numbers {#answer-keys-and-expected-numbers}

- Warm-up of Task 1: 1 = reproducibility (a failed attempt is still reproducibility); 2 = the grey area between reproducibility and robustness, argued both ways; 3 = replicability; 4 = generalisability.
- **Task 3, C6HJR** (`EUframes_cy.csv`, two-way fixed effects, conventional errors): b = −0.00347, SE = 0.00091, **t = −3.804**, df = 233, N = 270. Its conventional p is 0.0002, but under the rule of the course, CR2 errors clustered by country on 9.8 Satterthwaite df, p = 0.0504 (CR1 on 26 df 0.029; `cases/eu-frames/data/display_inference.csv`): not significant at 5% under that rule. Never call it significant without naming the errors.
- **Task 3, KQXUE** (`analyst_KQXUE.csv`, country fixed effects, conventional errors): b = −0.00736, SE = 0.00103, **t = −7.169**, df = 242, N = 270, CI from −0.00938 to −0.00533, as in the write-up of the analyst. With `cosmo_once` (EB 62.0 counted once) t = −7.166. On the Eurostat series as retrieved in 2026, in which Portugal 2013 reads 13.0 rather than 12.9, t = −7.172; the file uses the December 2023 vintage.
- **Task 3, 018OL** (`analyst_018OL.csv`, random intercepts for country, year and wave, Satterthwaite df): on the outcome rescaled to 0–1, b = −0.00203, SE = 0.00169, **t = −1.206**, df = 396.9, N = 420, as in the knitted output of the analyst; on the raw cell means b = −0.00072, SE = 0.00060, with the same t and df. With the year of the fieldwork for EB 79.3, t = −1.606. The default `parameters::model_parameters()` reports the residual df (414); `ci_method = "satterthwaite"` gives 396.9.
- **Hands-on 3a** (data-tools day): respondents behind each year of the course panel – 43,023 in 2004 (two waves for the fifteen older member states, one for the twelve newer), about 53,300 in each year with two waves (2005, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2012) and about 26,700 in each year with one (2006, 2007, 2009, 2013). In `analyst_KQXUE.csv` the 27 rows of 2004 have `n` above `n_once`, because EB 62.0 is counted twice. In `analyst_018OL.csv` the 27 cells of EB 79.3 have `year` 2012 and `year_fieldwork` 2013.
- **Hands-on 3b**: KQXUE, `task2.do`, `append using` the temporary file of EB 62.0 on two consecutive lines (441 and 442); 018OL, the line of the R Markdown file that sets `YEA` from the first four characters of the file name, commented "year of data collection"; C6HJR, the comment `# APRIL 2025 - Mistake in dataset here` in the corrected script of the fork. Good checks: no file read twice; one wave per fieldwork period with its expected count; counts by year and country; two builds compared cell by cell.
- The curve (methods day, `cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve.csv`): 864 specifications; 98.1% below zero; 77.2% below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 (conventional 90.3%, CR1 80.1%); claim-aligned r from −0.589 to +0.116, median −0.314. Country fixed effects 92.6% below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, two-way 61.8%.
- Few clusters (methods day, `display_inference.csv`): two-way fixed effects t = −3.80 on 233 df conventional, −2.31 on 26 df with CR1 (p = 0.029), −2.23 on 9.8 df with CR2 (p = 0.0504); country fixed effects on the course panel t = −6.87 on 242 df, −3.62 on 26 df, −3.51 on 8.5 df (p = 0.0072). Within and between (`display_between_within.csv`): −0.0056 within, +0.0041 across the 27 country means (p = 0.31), difference p = 0.024.
- Reference results (`cases/eu-frames/data/reference_marks.csv`), each placed on the degrees of freedom of its own inference, with the number of the 864 further below zero: KEVF1 −0.452 (147); KQXUE −0.419 (214); OA −0.385 (267, the refit of its design without the education interactions, t = −8.39 on 403.9 Satterthwaite df); C6HJR −0.242 (583); PRL47 −0.176 (740); 018OL −0.060 (833). Multi100 recorded PRL47 at −0.006, its z converted on 394,575 respondents.
- Fork importance (`spec_curve_forks.csv`), share of the variance: estimator 41.5%, predictor 16.9, outcome 9.0, adjustment 4.3, item set 3.1, no-opinion rule 0.9, series 0.1, cell weighting 0.0, form 0.0, interactions 24.1.
- Placement of the reproduced specification (for participants without their own submission): 67%, with 583 of the 864 further below zero.

## Debrief questions {#debrief-question-bank}

Choose by what the class actually produced, not by the order below.

1. **The three reproductions** (all formats): "Three analysts, one claim, the same instructions: −1.2, −3.8, −7.2. Which difference between their models matters most, and how would you find out?"
2. **The slips** (open science, data tools): "None of the three slips changed a conclusion. Does that make them unimportant? What would have to be true of a slip for it to matter?"
3. **The vintage** (open science, data tools): "A public series changed after the analysis. Whose job is it to keep the version that a result rests on?"
4. **The rule for success** (open science): "The class wrote different rules for the same replication. Which of them would count the SCORE replication as a success, and which would not?"
5. **Decision that moved most** (methods): "Before I showed the decomposition – which decision did you bet on, and what made the estimator carry so much?"
6. **Justification quality** (methods): "Whose graph settled their choice? Whose graph could have justified three different specifications equally well?"
7. **Preregistration felt** (methods): "Did completing the block before running change how the result felt when it landed?"
8. **The inference gap** (methods): "If a curve-level permutation test came back at p = .30, what would survive of today? What if it came back at p = .004?"
